meta.title: The Depot at the Center of Town
meta.intro: It is the 1890s. You are Ada Pruitt, 16, whose family farms cotton outside Woodstock. Make up to five choices and see how the railroad shaped the town you know today. About 5 minutes.
meta.characterNote: Ada Pruitt and her family are fictional composite characters. Places, dates and events marked “True history” come from the cited sources.

route.name: Dave Haney Home
route.blurb: Built circa 1908 and home to David J. and Edna McCleskey Haney for many years. Later occupants included Canton newspaper editor Joe Parham; J.E., S.L. and S.L. Johnston Jr. bought it, and in 1946 sold it to J.D. and Edison Whitmire, whose family lived here until 1979. The two-story house keeps much of its wrap-around porch with pilasters and Victorian-style woodwork.

quiz.q: Which family lived here from 1946 until 1979?

route.name: Linton Dean Home
route.blurb: Originally built circa 1918 for Claude Chandler, then bought by Linton Dean in 1931 for $3,000. He lived here with his wife Alice Wellons Dean and daughters Elizabeth and Alice. It is a craftsman bungalow with tapered square columns and a porte-cochère, and a badminton court on the back lawn drew young people to the home.

quiz.q: What did Linton Dean pay for the house in 1931?

route.name: Latimer-Howell Home
route.blurb: Built in 1906 for Wylie P. Dobbs and soon sold to Thomas E. Latimer for $100. His sister Martha Latimer owned it from 1907 to 1937. In 1943 L. E. Howell bought the house, and it stayed in the Howell family until 2001. Its Victorian style was enhanced when it was renovated for commercial use; the wide veranda once wrapped around two sides.

quiz.q: How long did the Howell family keep the house?

route.name: Woodstock School
route.blurb: The older section—two wings joined by a gymnasium/auditorium—survived the 1939 fire that destroyed the original schoolhouse. The addition built after the fire has a bell cupola still in evidence, and other facilities came in the 1960s. The school relocated in 2005, and Chattahoochee Technical College occupies the campus today.

quiz.q: What happened to the original schoolhouse in 1939?

route.name: Emmett Dial Home
route.blurb: Built for Emmett Dial about 1910 and first occupied by Mr. Dial, his sister and brother-in-law. Later he married Mary Claude Simpson, and they lived here until their deaths; their only child, Sara Frances, was born in the home. Mr. Dial was Woodstock's postmaster from 1917 to 1933. Look for the front porch that curves gracefully to one side and the clipped gable roofline.

quiz.q: What job did Emmett Dial hold from 1917 to 1933?

route.name: W.D. Bozeman Home
route.blurb: Built circa 1910 by L. J. Runyon and first occupied by the W. D. Bozeman family; three of the four Bozeman daughters kept living here, and the last passed away in 2003. The white prairie-style house has four square 4-over-4 double-hung sash windows, a corner tower, a bay window and a vintage staircase 27 inches wide.

quiz.q: How wide is the vintage staircase?

route.name: Woodstock Presbyterian Church
route.blurb: The original Bethesda Presbyterian Church north of Woodstock burned in 1916. In 1923 it relocated, was renamed Woodstock Presbyterian Church, and this building went up; the congregation used it until 1989. The decorative woodwork under the gables is unique to the town, and in fall a yellow maple lights up the steeple.

quiz.q: What was the church called before it moved in 1923?

route.name: W.L. Dean Home
route.blurb: Built circa 1875; Dr. William Lemuel and Lou Boring Dean lived here beginning in 1883, and their seven children were born here. The architecture recalls an English cottage. The bricks were made in the yard, the front porch columns came from the Canton hotel, and ivy planted over the front bay window in 1885 thrived for years.

quiz.q: Where did the front porch columns come from?

route.name: J.H. Johnston Home
route.blurb: Built in 1913 after the original wood house burned along with nearby Woodstock Baptist Church. Mr. Johnston was a local merchant and founder of the Bank of Woodstock. He married Avis Benson and they had ten children; their son Joseph E. Johnston lived here until his death in 1978. Note the six Ionic columns on the front porch.

quiz.q: How many Ionic columns are on the front porch?

route.name: Woodstock Baptist Church
route.blurb: Originally Enon Baptist Church, north of town; the congregation moved into town in 1879. In 1884 it was renamed Woodstock Baptist Church and a new meeting house was built. That burned in 1913 and was replaced by this sanctuary, with a flat bell tower, no steeple, and arched stained-glass windows that once swiveled open. The bricks match the Johnston House next door. The congregation moved in 1991.

quiz.q: Why do this church's bricks match the house next door?
options: Same builder's bricks as the Johnston House

route.name: Post Office
route.blurb: Woodstock had postmasters as early as 1833, with mail handled in homes or businesses. This building, constructed circa 1908, was the first used only as a post office. John T. Morgan, postmaster 1909–1915, was also a builder. A faux stone facade covers the original brick storefront. In 1961 the post office moved to 8604/8606 Main St., and W. H. Howard later ran Woodstock Jewelry here.

quiz.q: Before this building, where was Woodstock's mail handled?

route.name: Cotton Warehouse
route.blurb: The J. H. Johnston cotton warehouse, circa 1905, is the last of several such warehouses in Woodstock. Cotton was stored on the upper floor, which opened onto Church Street; crews moved 500-pound bales from wagons, and each bale was weighed and tagged with a receipt for weight, date and quality. The basement was too humid for cotton, so fertilizer and plows were kept there.

quiz.q: Why was cotton kept upstairs instead of in the basement?

route.name: Woodstock Methodist Church
route.blurb: Home to the oldest church in continuous operation in the same building in the city. Built in 1889, with major improvements in 1924 including brick walls. A 1953 redesign added Sunday School rooms, a basement, a kitchen and restrooms. Stained-glass windows and stately trees add to its charm.

quiz.q: When was this church building constructed?

route.name: Bank of Woodstock
route.blurb: Before 1908 this was the site of a livery stable. J. H. Johnston built the current structure in 1908 for the Bank of Woodstock, which stayed until 1972 when it moved to 8770 Main St. From 1972 to 1989 the building housed the Woodstock Public Library. Note the golden brick and decorative brickwork; 1970s photos showed a hitching post on the Church Street side.

quiz.q: What stood on this site before 1908?

route.name: Dobbs-Chandler Building
route.blurb: Built by Amanda Chandler Edwards circa 1905. The first business here was a grocery and general merchandise store run by Claude Chandler. Later came Hendon Grocery, Williams Food Store, Dawson-Parr Department Store, and Keenum's Gift and Toyland.

quiz.q: What kind of store came first?
options: A grocery and general merchandise store

route.name: Dean's Store
route.blurb: This building and 8582 Main St. were presumably built at the same time, with matching facades, roof lines and a common wall; it dates to circa 1905 or earlier. Owner Dr. W. H. Dean was one of the town's original settlers. His son Dr. Will Dean opened Dean's Drug Store here in 1906 with his son Linton Dean, who ran it until his death in 1981. Today the intact store is home to the Woodstock Visitors Center.

quiz.q: What is in Dean's Store today?

route.name: Woodstock Depot
route.blurb: Built in 1912 to replace the first depot, which was later demolished. It has tongue-and-groove siding and a red clay tile roof—typical North Georgia railroad depot architecture with Victorian-era influence—and served as a combination station for freight and passengers. The depot and tracks were the center of the city's original boundaries in the 1897 charter. It is the only structure in Woodstock on the National Register of Historic Places.

quiz.q: What was measured from the depot in the 1897 charter?

route.name: Original Location of J.H. Johnston Company
route.blurb: Believed to be the first location of the J. H. Johnston Company, General Mercantile and Cotton Brokers, established in 1888 and the major business in Woodstock for eight decades. The Woodstock Masonic Lodge used the second floor until recent years, along with the telephone exchange. The Bank of Woodstock began here before moving to its new building in 1908.

quiz.q: Which bank started inside this store?

route.name: Chandler Building
route.blurb: Mack Dobbs is believed to have been the first owner, circa 1913. He ran a funeral parlor here with partner Claude Chandler, and a mule-drawn hearse was kept on the premises. Ernest Thompson later reportedly had a used Ford parts business, and in the 1970s Riley Medley ran a family restaurant. The cast iron Meskers on either side of the double front doors, with a fleur-de-lis design, are unique in Woodstock.

quiz.q: What pulled the funeral parlor's hearse?

route.name: Jail
route.blurb: Originally a brick building where L. J. Runyon carved monuments circa 1914. It was a cannery during World War II and became city property in 1952. The fire truck was parked here and it was known as Old City Hall; later occupants used "Olde Towne Hall" as a business name. Bars on a single window recall the days it held prisoners before transfer to the county jail.

quiz.q: What was this building used for during World War II?

route.name: Johnston-Neese Home
route.blurb: Traces its origin to J. H. Johnston circa 1890. His son Walt Johnston lived here, then retired Methodist minister John Wesley Gober. The Smith L. Johnston Jr. family moved in in the late 1940s. Doc Neese bought it in 1954 and it stayed with the Neese family until 1985, when the William Johnston family became owners. Look for Queen Anne elements and a street-level porch with decorative woodwork.

quiz.q: Who bought the house in 1954?

route.name: S.L. Johnston Home
route.blurb: Soon after their marriage in 1917, Smith Lemon Johnston and Florine Dial moved into this new brick craftsman-style bungalow, designed by a friend and built for $1,700. Their four children grew up here; after Mrs. Johnston's death it became the home of the youngest son, William J. Johnston. Its structure has been carefully maintained.

quiz.q: What did the bungalow cost to build?

route.name: Sam Dawson Home
route.blurb: Built in 1909 by Sam and Georgia Carpenter Dawson, originally surrounded by porches on all sides. Sliding pocket doors led from the reception hall to the parlor, and the dining room sat in the center of the house with no windows. Original fireplaces and mantels remain, and the basic design can still be seen.

quiz.q: What was unusual about the dining room?

route.name: W.D. Power Home
route.blurb: Built in 1912 for Walter Dean Power and his bride Nellie Dobbs: a white frame house with a brick foundation, twelve-foot ceilings, a colonnade between living and dining rooms, and a wide pine staircase to the bedrooms. Each of the three Power children was born in the ground-floor bedroom. The yard had a garage, a stable for a horse and cow, and later a tennis court. The Power family lived here for ninety years.

quiz.q: How long did the Power family live here?

route.name: Olde Rope Mill Park
route.address: Rope Mill Rd., about 1 mile north of downtown
route.maps: Olde Rope Mill Park, Woodstock, GA
route.blurb: Since the 1840s and maybe earlier, grist mills worked this stretch of Little River. The 1880 census lists the Joel T. Haley mill making cotton yarns using the river's slight drop for power. The final cotton mill, Rope Mill (1928–1949), made rope for wells, plow lines and tents; Joe Johnston and Smith Johnston Sr. were the last owners. It closed in 1949 after the U.S. Government bought the land for Allatoona Lake. Ruins and signs are in the park today.

quiz.q: What did Rope Mill make from 1928 to 1949?
options: Rope for wells, plow lines and tents

s1.title: Harvest at the Tracks
text: Your father's wagon creaks toward the depot with bales of cotton. Before the trains came, families here mostly grew what they needed. Now the rails run straight through the village.
Father hands you the reins. “You decide where we take this load first.”
s1.fact: The Marietta & North Georgia Railroad reached Woodstock in 1879 on its line from Marietta to Canton. A first depot stood on the west side of the tracks, and farmers used the line to ship cotton to mills. (Today's depot at this stop replaced that first depot in 1912.)

choices.label: Go to the depot and ship the cotton by rail
Stop at the big general store on Main Street

s2a.title: The Depot Agent
text: The depot agent tallies your bales, and the telegraph clicks behind him. Trains carry mail, goods and passengers to Marietta and beyond.
A man on the platform says the town may soon become an official city.
s2a.fact: The depot was the focal point for shipping cotton, rope and farm products, and for travelers heading to Canton and Marietta. It had an agent and telegraph service.

choices.label: Ask the man what becoming a city would mean

s2b.title: Johnston's Store
text: Main Street is lined with businesses on its west side, and cotton warehouses stand across the way. At the J.H. Johnston Company you can sell your cotton and buy supplies in the same trip.
The clerk mentions talk of a town charter.
s2b.fact: This is believed to be the first location of the J.H. Johnston Company, General Mercantile and Cotton Brokers, established in 1888. The Woodstock Masonic Lodge and the telephone exchange used the second floor, and the Bank of Woodstock began in the store before moving to its own building in 1908.

choices.label: Ask the clerk about the charter

s3.title: A Town Measured from the Depot
text: News arrives: the Georgia legislature has granted Woodstock a charter. Folks gather to hear how the new town lines were drawn.
Everyone laughs when they hear where the measuring started.
s3.fact: On December 8, 1897, the Georgia legislature chartered Woodstock. City limits ran ¾ mile north and south of the depot and ½ mile east and west of the tracks, making the depot the center of town. Nathan Fowler was the first mayor. The 1900 census counted 276 residents.
s3.prompt: Years pass. Where does your future lead?

choices.label: Stay in town and help with the family's cotton business
Look for work at the mill on Little River

s_wh.title: Weighing Day at the Warehouse
text: You drive the wagon up to the Johnston cotton warehouse on Church Street. A work crew wrestles each heavy bale off the wagon and onto the scale.
The clerk hands you a receipt. Down on Main Street, Dr. W.H. Dean's store is open for business. Your father asks what to do with the money.
s_wh.fact: The J.H. Johnston cotton warehouse, built around 1905, is the last of several such warehouses in Woodstock. Crews moved 500-pound bales by hand into the upper floor, which opened onto Church Street. Each bale was weighed and tagged, and the owner got a receipt showing weight, date and quality. The humid basement held fertilizer, plows and other farm equipment instead. Dean's Store at 8588 Main St. was built around 1905 or earlier; Dr. W.H. Dean was the owner, and the building is now the Woodstock Visitors Center.

choices.label: Save it and watch the town grow around the depot
Buy a new plow from the warehouse basement

s4.title: A New Depot
text: You are grown now. Crews finish a new wooden depot beside the tracks, with a red clay tile roof, a freight room and a passenger waiting area.
Your niece asks whether to ride the train to school in Canton or Marietta.
s4.fact: The Louisville & Nashville Railroad bought the line in 1905 and built the current depot in 1912 on the east side of the tracks, replacing the first depot, which was later torn down. It has tongue-and-groove siding and a red clay tile roof, typical North Georgia depot design with Victorian touches, and served as a “combination station” for freight and passengers. Like other L&N depots of the time, it had a separate entrance and waiting room for Black passengers under segregation.

choices.label: Tell her to take the train to school
Tell her to stay and build something in Woodstock

s4m.title: The Mill on Little River
text: North of town, Little River drops just enough to turn a mill wheel, and the mill spins local cotton. The work is loud and long, but the pay is steady.
A foreman asks if you will train the new hands.
s4m.fact: Grist mills worked this stretch of Little River from the 1840s or earlier. The 1880 census shows the Joel T. Haley mill making cotton yarns, using the river's slight drop to power textile machinery. A series of owners and cotton businesses followed.

choices.label: Return to town and the depot

e_rails.title: Ending: The Line to the Wider World
text: Your niece rides the train to school each day, part of a generation the rails connected to wider Georgia.
history: Students rode the train from the Woodstock depot to school in Canton and Marietta. Passenger service ended on March 1, 1949, and the depot kept freight and telegraph service until the late 1950s.

e_town.title: Ending: The Center Still Holds
text: Your family stays and helps the little town grow around its depot.
history: The 1912 depot still stands and is on the National Register of Historic Places, the only such listing in Woodstock. Main Street was paved in 1912. Woodstock grew from about 4,500 to about 36,000 residents over three decades.

e_mill.title: Ending: Cotton into Rope
text: You become one of the experienced hands at the mill, teaching others the trade as owners come and go.
history: The last cotton mill on the site, Rope Mill (1928–1949), made rope for wells, plow lines and tents. Joe Johnston and Smith Johnston Sr. were its last owners. It closed in 1949 after the U.S. Government bought the property for Lake Allatoona. Ruins of the mill and history signs are in Olde Rope Mill Park today.
